stops.name: Bloemfontein, the birthplace on the high veldt
stops.campa: On the third of January, in the parched capital of the Orange Free State, John Ronald Reuel Tolkien is born to Arthur, an English bank manager, and Mabel his wife. The land is bare and hot, a wide emptiness of dust and enormous sky; the child's first world is the blank horizon and the stars strewn thick above it. Into the bank-house garden a great hairy spider comes and bites the toddling boy; his nurse sucks out the venom. The wound heals, the memory sinks, but the dry plains and the crawling terror both go down into the deep well from which Rohan and Shelob will one day rise.

stops.name: The Cathedral church, Bloemfontein: christened John Ronald Reuel
stops.campa: On the last day of January the infant is carried to the Anglican cathedral of the frontier town and christened John Ronald Reuel: Reuel a family name he never fully explains, which he will hand on to his own son. Arthur, prospering at the bank, means to raise his boys in Africa. But the harsh climate wastes the elder child, and within three years Mabel sails home to Birmingham for their health, leaving Arthur to follow. He never does: in February 1896 rheumatic fever and a brain haemorrhage take him, and he is buried at Bloemfontein, an ocean from his sons. The boy is fatherless at four.

stops.name: Sarehole Mill, the green heart of the Shire
stops.campa: Mabel brings her two boys home to England, and after Arthur dies in Africa she settles them at Sarehole, a Worcestershire hamlet beneath a great water-mill. Here the exile of the veldt is answered: a lost paradise of meadow, millpond and the wooded bog. The boy roams with his brother Hilary, dreads the white-dusted miller's son they call the White Ogre, filches mushrooms from the farmer's field. Mabel teaches them at home: Latin, botany, the look and feel of trees. This bright, small English country, held only four years, becomes forever the model of the Shire, the homeland worth defending.
stops.quote: I could draw you a map of every inch of it. I loved it with an (idealised) love.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on Sarehole, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: The Birmingham Oratory and Rednal, the mother's death
stops.campa: Mabel, received into the Roman Church in 1900, is cut off by her Baptist kin for it, and sinks into poverty and illness. In the summer she lodges the boys in a cottage at Rednal by the Oratory's country house. There, on the fourteenth of November, in a diabetic coma, she dies at thirty-four. Ronald is twelve. He holds her ever after as a martyr who gave her life for the faith she would not renounce, and from her death he draws a lifelong grief-bright Catholicism, and the conviction woven through all his work that the world is fallen, its truest note the long defeat lit by sudden joy.
stops.quote: My own dear mother was a martyr indeed, and it is not to everybody that God grants so easy a way to his great gifts as he did to Hilary and myself, giving us a mother who killed herself with labour and trouble to ensure us keeping the faith.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 267 (to Michael Tolkien)

stops.name: King Edward's School, Birmingham: the philologist forged
stops.campa: On a Foundation Scholarship the orphan enters the great grammar school under the shadow of the two towers of the Oratory. Here his gift declares itself: Latin and Greek, then Anglo-Saxon, Gothic, Middle English, the Welsh names glimpsed on Welsh coal-trucks that he finds heart-piercingly beautiful. He begins, in boyhood, to invent tongues: first playful nonsense, then true grammars with sound-laws and histories. He is caught not by the meaning of words but by their music; 'cellar door', he will say, is a beautiful sound. Language is not his tool but his desire; the mythology, he confesses, is made to give his languages a world to be spoken in.
stops.quote: The invention of languages is the foundation. The 'stories' were made rather to provide a world for the languages than the reverse.

stops.name: The railway sidings, the Welsh names on the coal-trucks
stops.campa: Along the Birmingham lines the coal-trucks come up from the valleys of South Wales bearing painted names: Nantyglo, Senghenydd, Blaen-Rhondda, Penrhiwceiber. And the boy reads them from the embankment as a kind of enchantment. He cannot understand a word, yet the shapes and sounds pierce him with a longing he cannot name, a beauty in the very grain of the language. This first wound of Welsh never closes; decades on it flowers into Sindarin, the Grey-elven tongue, patterned on the music of Welsh. His languages are born of desire before they are ever built of grammar.
stops.quote: The fluidity of Welsh, with peculiar phonetic charm . . . its 'wildness and beauty' appeals to me.

stops.name: 37 Duchess Road, Edith Bratt across the landing
stops.campa: Father Francis Morgan, guardian of the orphaned brothers, lodges them in a boarding-house where a fellow lodger is Edith Bratt, herself an orphan, three years older, a fine pianist. The two conspire: they haunt Birmingham teashops, sit on a balcony above the street, and drop sugar-lumps into the hats of passers-by. By the summer of 1909 they are in love. It is a first, secret, whole-hearted love, and it will echo down the years into a tale of a mortal man and an immortal maid who dances in a wood, the greatest of the stories of the Elder Days.

stops.name: Barrow's Stores, the Tea Club and Barrovian Society
stops.campa: In the school library and in the tea-room of Barrow's Stores four boys form a secret fellowship, brewing clandestine tea and reading their poems and enthusiasms aloud. They are Tolkien, Christopher Wiseman, Robert Gilson, and Geoffrey Bache Smith: the T.C.B.S., the Tea Club and Barrovian Society, the 'immortal four'. They believe themselves called to kindle a new light in the world through art and letters. This brotherhood is the first Fellowship of his life: a company of friends bound by love and high purpose. The war will shatter it, and out of that shattering the mythology will be born.

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford, the undergraduate philologist
stops.campa: Tolkien comes up to Exeter College on an Open Classical Exhibition, but Classics cannot hold him. He steeps himself in Old English, Gothic, Welsh, and above all Finnish, the strange sweet tongue of the Kalevala, over which he pores until his examinations suffer. After a merely good Second in Honour Moderations he changes his school to English Language and Literature. In the Finnish grammar he finds the seed of a new invented language, high and vowel-rich, that he begins to build in his notebooks. He does not yet know that this Qenya will become the Latin of the Elves, the tongue of the Valinorean lords.
stops.quote: It was like discovering a complete wine-cellar filled with bottles of an amazing wine of a kind and flavour never tasted before. It quite intoxicated me.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on first reading Finnish, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: Cheltenham, the reunion at the railway station
stops.campa: On the very night of his twenty-first birthday, freed at last from his guardian's ban, Tolkien writes to Edith, now removed to Cheltenham, to say he loves her still and to ask her hand. She writes back that she is engaged to another. Within a week he takes the train to Cheltenham; she meets him on the platform. Before the day is out she returns her ring to the farmer and pledges herself instead to Ronald. The lovers, parted three years by an old priest's command, are joined again, and the pattern of Beren winning back Lúthien from a hopeless case is quietly, life-long, laid down.

stops.name: The Crist of Cynewulf: Éarendel, brightest of angels
stops.campa: Reading the Old English Crist of Cynewulf, Tolkien is stopped and shaken by a line: Eala Earendel engla beorhtast, ofer middangeard monnum sended, 'Hail Earendel, brightest of angels, above the middle-earth sent unto men.' A strange thrill runs through him, as if something long asleep had stirred. He feels behind the word a whole lost world he must recover. From this single line grows Earendil the Mariner, who sails his ship into the sky bearing a Silmaril as the morning star, and Middle-earth itself takes its name from that ancient poem's middangeard.
stops.quote: There was something very remote and strange and beautiful behind those words, if I could grasp it, far beyond ancient English.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on the Éarendel line, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: St Mary Immaculate, Warwick, the marriage
stops.campa: With the Somme gathering on the horizon and his commission already in hand, Tolkien marries Edith Bratt in the Catholic church of St Mary Immaculate at Warwick, beneath its castle. She has become a Catholic to marry him. They have a few weeks together before he must go. Warwick, with its castle and its old town, is for him already half-mythical, a town glimpsed as through a haze into a lost age; in his early poems it becomes Kortirion, the city of the fading Elves. Man and wife, they stand at the edge of the abyss into which his generation is about to fall.
